## Why K-Dramas Are the Best Korean Teacher

If you've watched more than 10 minutes of a Korean drama, you've already started learning Korean without knowing it. The same phrases come up again and again: and once you recognize them, you can't unhear them.

Research shows that learners who combine drama watching with structured study pick up vocabulary 40% faster than textbook-only learners. The emotional context of dramatic scenes creates stronger memory connections.

Here are 30 essential phrases straight from your favorite shows, organized by situation: with pronunciation, formality level, and exactly when you'll hear them.

---

## Greetings & Daily Life

**1. 안녕하세요 (annyeonghaseyo)**: *Hello*
Formality: Polite. Used with anyone: strangers, elders, colleagues.
Drama moment: The opening line of almost every first meeting scene.

**2. 안녕 (annyeong)**: *Hi / Bye*
Formality: Casual. Only with close friends or people younger than you.
Drama moment: Friends greeting each other at school or cafés.

**3. 잘 지냈어요? (jal jinaesseoyo?)**: *How have you been?*
Literally: "Have you been doing well?" Used after not seeing someone for a while.
Drama moment: Every time characters reunite after a time skip.

**4. 오랜만이에요 (oraenmanieyo)**: *Long time no see*
Drama moment: Episode 1 of any drama where childhood friends meet as adults.

**5. 밥 먹었어요? (bap meogeosseoyo?)**: *Have you eaten?*
This is NOT just about food. Koreans use this as a way of saying "I care about you." It's like asking "How are you?" in Korean culture.
Arabic equivalent: Similar to how Egyptians say "اتغديت؟" (did you have lunch?) as a greeting.

**6. 다녀오겠습니다 (danyeo-ogetseumnida)**: *I'm heading out (and will be back)*
Said when leaving home. The response is 다녀와 (danyeowa): "come back safely."
Drama moment: Every scene where someone leaves for work or school.

---

## Emotions & Reactions

**7. 진짜요? (jinjjayo?)**: *Really? Seriously?*
Said with wide eyes in every drama ever. The casual version is 진짜? (jinjja?).
Usage frequency: You'll hear this at least 10 times per episode.

**8. 대박 (daebak)**: *Awesome / No way!*
An exclamation of surprise or amazement. Originally meant "jackpot."
Drama moment: When something unexpectedly good (or shocking) happens.

**9. 아이고 (aigo)**: *Oh my / Oh no*
Arabic equivalent: Like "يا إلهي" (ya ilahi) or "يا لهوي" (ya lahwy) in Egyptian Arabic.
Used by everyone but especially Korean grandmothers. Expresses surprise, frustration, exhaustion, or affection.

**10. 어떡해 (eotteokae)**: *What do I do? / Oh no!*
The ultimate Korean panic phrase. Said while clutching face or pacing.
Drama moment: When the protagonist discovers a devastating secret.

**11. 설레다 (seolleda)**: *To have butterflies / feel excited about someone*
The Korean word for that fluttery feeling at the beginning of a romance. No exact English or Arabic equivalent.
Drama moment: Every romantic subplot, usually with a soft piano soundtrack.

**12. 미치겠다 (michigetda)**: *I'm going crazy*
Used when frustrated, overwhelmed, or when someone is driving you insane (in love or anger).
Drama moment: At least once per episode in any thriller or romance.

---

## Romance (Essential for K-Drama Fans)

**13. 사랑해 (saranghae)**: *I love you* (casual)
The formal version is 사랑합니다 (saranghamnida). Usually saved for the climax of a romance.
Drama moment: Usually said in the rain, at an airport, or on a rooftop.

**14. 보고 싶어 (bogo sipeo)**: *I miss you*
Literally: "I want to see you." One of the most romantic Korean phrases.
Drama moment: Phone calls between separated lovers.

**15. 손 잡아도 돼요? (son jabado dwaeyo?)**: *Can I hold your hand?*
The classic Korean first-touch scene. Korean dramas often make hand-holding the emotional peak of early romance.

**16. 내 옆에 있어줘 (nae yeope isseojwo)**: *Stay by my side*
Romantic and dramatic. Often said during vulnerable moments.

**17. 운명이야 (unmyeongiya)**: *It's destiny / fate*
Said when leads realize they keep bumping into each other. Korean dramas love the concept of 운명 (unmyeong, fate/destiny).
Arabic connection: Similar to the Arabic concept of "نصيب" (naseeb): destiny bringing two people together.

**18. 좋아해요 (joahaeyo)**: *I like you*

Saying "I can" or "I can't" do something is one of the first practical grammar patterns every Korean learner needs: and it follows one clean, consistent structure across nearly every verb.

## The Basic Pattern: -을/ㄹ 수 있다/없다

Attach -을 수 있다 (can) or -을 수 없다 (cannot) to a verb stem, choosing -을 or -ㄹ depending on whether the stem ends in a consonant or vowel.

| Stem ends in | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Consonant | -을 수 있어요 | -을 수 없어요 |
| Vowel | -ㄹ 수 있어요 | -ㄹ 수 없어요 |

Examples:
- 저는 한국어를 할 수 있어요.: I can speak Korean.
- 저는 매운 음식을 먹을 수 없어요.: I can't eat spicy food.
- 그는 피아노를 칠 수 있어요.: He can play the piano.

## Asking About Ability

- 수영할 수 있어요?: Can you swim?
- 이거 오늘까지 끝낼 수 있어요?: Can you finish this by today?

## -을 줄 알다/모르다: Learned Skill vs General Ability

A related but distinct pattern, -을 줄 알다 (know how to) and -을 줄 모르다 (don't know how to), specifically emphasizes a learned skill rather than general possibility.

| Pattern | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 운전할 줄 알아요. | I know how to drive. (learned skill) |
| 운전할 수 있어요. | I can drive. (ability, possibly circumstantial) |

In many everyday contexts these overlap, but -을 줄 알다 specifically highlights that you learned the skill, while -을 수 있다 is broader and can include temporary circumstances too (예: 오늘은 차가 있어서 갈 수 있어요: I can go today because I have a car).

## Common Mistakes to Avoid

1. **Forgetting the consonant/vowel rule.** Using -을 with a vowel-ending stem (or vice versa) is one of the most frequent beginner slip-ups.
2. **Mixing up 수 있다 and 줄 알다 carelessly.** They are close in meaning but not always interchangeable: 수 있다 is the safer default for general "can" statements.

## Quick FAQ

**Is there a past tense version?** Yes: 할 수 있었어요 (could/was able to) and 할 수 없었어요 (couldn't/was not able to).

**How do I say "maybe I can"?** Add -을/ㄹ 수도 있어요 (there's also a possibility that...) for a softer, less certain statement of ability or possibility.

Ability expressions unlock so much real conversation: describing skills, negotiating deadlines, talking about hobbies. Klovers' lessons give you practice using this pattern.

Adjectives do the heavy lifting in daily Korean. They describe your mood, the weather, K-drama leads, and Seoul street food. This list of **korean adjectives** gives you 100 must-know words split into useful categories, each with romanization, meaning, and a real example sentence.

One important note: in Korean, adjectives are actually *descriptive verbs*: they conjugate like verbs. Dictionary form ends in 다; spoken form typically ends in 아요 / 어요.

## How Korean Adjectives Work

- Dictionary: 예쁘다 (yeppeuda): to be pretty
- Polite: 예뻐요 (yeppeoyo): is pretty
- Modifier (before nouns): 예쁜 + noun: pretty thing

The modifier form uses -은/-ㄴ after the stem.

## 1. Describing People (Appearance)

| Korean | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 예쁘다 | pretty | 그 배우는 예뻐요 |
| 잘생기다 | handsome | 오빠가 정말 잘생겼어요 |
| 귀엽다 | cute | 강아지가 귀여워요 |
| 멋있다 | cool / stylish | 이 남자는 멋있어요 |
| 키가 크다 | tall | 저는 키가 커요 |
| 날씬하다 | slim | 친구는 날씬해요 |
| 통통하다 | chubby | 고양이가 통통해요 |

## 2. Describing Personality

- 친절하다 (chinjeolhada): kind: 사장님이 친절해요
- 착하다 (chakhada): good-hearted
- 똑똑하다 (ttokttokhada): smart
- 재미있다 (jaemiitda): fun, interesting
- 지루하다 (jiruhada): boring
- 조용하다 (joyonghada): quiet
- 활발하다 (hwalbalhada): outgoing
- 게으르다 (geeureuda): lazy
- 성실하다: diligent
- 이기적이다: selfish

## 3. Emotions and Feelings

- 행복하다 (haengbokhada): happy
- 슬프다 (seulpeuda): sad
- 화나다: angry
- 피곤하다 (pigonhada): tired
- 심심하다: bored
- 놀랍다: surprising
- 걱정되다: worried
- 부끄럽다: embarrassed
- 외롭다: lonely
- 설레다 (seolleda): to feel fluttery, excited (K-drama gold)

Example: 오늘 너무 행복해요: I am so happy today.

## 4. Describing Food

| Korean | Meaning | Example |
|---|---|---|
| 맛있다 | delicious | 김치찌개가 맛있어요 |
| 맛없다 | not tasty | 이 빵은 맛없어요 |
| 맵다 | spicy | 떡볶이가 매워요 |
| 짜다 | salty | 국이 짜요 |
| 달다 | sweet | 케이크가 달아요 |
| 시다 | sour | 레몬이 셔요 |
| 쓰다 | bitter | 커피가 써요 |
| 고소하다 | nutty / savory | 참기름이 고소해요 |
| 느끼하다 | greasy | 피자가 느끼해요 |
| 뜨겁다 | hot (temperature) | 국이 뜨거워요 |
| 차갑다 | cold | 물이 차가워요 |

## 5. Weather and Nature

- 덥다: hot
- 춥다: cold
- 따뜻하다: warm
- 시원하다: cool
- 맑다: clear
- 흐리다: cloudy
- 건조하다: dry
- 습하다: humid
- 아름답다: beautiful
- 조용하다: quiet (place)

Example: 오늘 날씨가 맑아요: Today the weather is clear.

## 6. Size, Shape, and Quantity

- 크다: big: 집이 커요
- 작다: small
- 길다: long
- 짧다: short
- 높다: high
- 낮다: low
- 두껍다: thick
- 얇다: thin
- 넓다: wide
- 좁다: narrow
- 많다: many
- 적다: few

## 7. Quality and Condition

- 좋다: good
- 나쁘다: bad
- 새롭다: new
- 오래되다: old (thing)
- 깨끗하다: clean
- 더럽다: dirty
- 쉽다: easy
- 어렵다: difficult
- 빠르다: fast
- 느리다: slow
- 비싸다: expensive
- 싸다: cheap

These change form when conjugated: worth memorizing early.

| 예쁘다 | 예뻤어요 | 예쁜 |
| 바쁘다 | 바빴어요 | 바쁜 |

## Why Are Koreans Always Older Than You Think?

If you have ever chatted with a Korean person and asked their age, you may have gotten a confusing answer. "I am 25: but by the international count, I am 23."

**Quick answer:** Traditional Korean age counts you as 1 at birth and adds a year every 1 January, so it is one or two years above your international age (만 나이). Since 28 June 2023, South Korean law and administration use international age by default, with a few exceptions such as military service, school entry and buying alcohol or tobacco.

Welcome to the Korean age system: one of the most unique cultural features of Korea and one of the most common sources of confusion for Korean learners.

## Three Age Systems in Korea

Korea actually uses three different age systems depending on the context:

### 1. Korean Age (한국 나이: Hanguk Nai)
The traditional system. Everyone is born at age 1: not 0: and gains a year on January 1st, not on their birthday.

This means:
- A baby born on December 31st is 1 year old on the day they are born
- The very next day (January 1st), they become 2 years old
- By international standards, this baby is 2 days old

### 2. International Age (만 나이: Man Nai)
The standard age system used globally. You are born at 0 and gain a year on your birthday. South Korea made it the default for legal and administrative purposes from 28 June 2023.

### 3. Year Age (연 나이: Yeon Nai)
Used for some legal purposes, like military service, school enrollment and the age limits for buying alcohol and tobacco. Calculated simply as: current year minus birth year, with no month adjustment.

## How to Calculate Your Korean Age

**Korean age formula:**
Current year − Birth year + 1 = Korean age

Example: Born in 2000, current year 2026
2026 − 2000 + 1 = **27 Korean age**

Your birthday does not change this result: everyone born in the same year has the same Korean age all year long.

Actually it is simpler to just remember: **Korean age = international age + 1 or + 2** depending on whether your birthday has passed this year.

## Why Does This System Exist?

The Korean age system comes from ancient East Asian counting traditions shared with China and Japan (though both countries abandoned it decades ago).

One popular explanation: time spent in the womb counts. A baby born is already approximately 1 year old because they have been alive for 9 months before birth.

Additionally, gaining age collectively on January 1st (New Year's Day) has cultural significance: everyone grows older together, which aligns with Korea's collectivist cultural values where individual timelines are less important than shared community milestones.

## Worked Examples: One Person, Three Ages

Here is how the three systems compare on 1 October 2026:

| Birthday | International age (만 나이) | Year age (연 나이) | Traditional Korean age |
|----------|---------------------------|-------------------|------------------------|
| 15 March 2000 | 26 | 26 | 27 |
| 20 December 2000 | 25 | 26 | 27 |
| 1 January 2008 | 18 | 18 | 19 |
| 30 December 2025 | 0 | 1 | 2 |

Two patterns to notice:
- Year age is always traditional Korean age minus 1.
- International age equals year age once your birthday has passed this year, and is one less before it.

To say these ages aloud, use native Korean numbers with 살: 18 = 열여덟 살, 19 = 열아홉 살, 25 = 스물다섯 살, 26 = 스물여섯 살, 27 = 스물일곱 살.

## Age in Korean Social Dynamics

Understanding age in Korea is not just a math exercise: it has profound social implications.

**왜 나이를 물어봐요? (Why do Koreans ask your age?)**

In Korean culture, influenced by Confucian hierarchies, age determines:
- How you speak to someone (formal vs informal speech)
- Who pays at a meal (usually the oldest)
- Who speaks first in group settings
- How you are addressed

This is why Koreans ask age very early in a friendship: they need to know how to speak to you.

### Key Age-Related Vocabulary

| Korean | Romanization | Meaning |
|--------|-------------|---------|
| 나이 | na-i | age |
| 몇 살이에요? | myeot sal-i-e-yo | How old are you? (polite) |
| 저는 ~살이에요 | jeoneun ~sal-i-e-yo | I am ~ years old |
| 동갑이에요 | dong-gap-i-e-yo | We are the same age |
| 오빠/언니 | oppa/eonni | older brother/sister (familiar) |
| 선배/후배 | seonbae/hubae | senior/junior (school or work) |

## The 2023 Legal Reform

On 28 June 2023, South Korea's "man nai" unification law took effect. Unless a specific law says otherwise, ages in administrative and civil matters, such as official documents, laws and contracts, are now calculated in Man Nai (international age). A few areas still use year age, including military service, school entry and the age limits for buying alcohol and tobacco.

However, in everyday social conversation, Koreans still commonly use the traditional Korean age system. Old habits: especially ones tied to social hierarchy: do not change overnight.

## How to Talk About Age in Korean

When someone asks your age in Korean:
- **몇 살이에요?** (polite): How old are you?
- **저는 스물다섯 살이에요**: I am 25 years old (using native Korean numbers for age)
- **만으로는 스물셋이에요**: By international count, I am 23

Note: Age in Korean uses **native Korean numbers** (하나 둘 셋...) not Sino-Korean numbers (일 이 삼...).

At Klovers, we cover the Korean number systems, age expressions, and speech levels in Level 1: because you cannot have a real Korean conversation without understanding how age shapes every interaction. If you already know some Korean, take the free [placement test](/placement-test) to find your level.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### Does South Korea still use Korean age?
Officially, international age (만 나이) has been the default in law and administration since 28 June 2023. Year age is still used for a few things, such as military service, school entry and the alcohol and tobacco age limits, and some people still mention their traditional Korean age in conversation.

### How do I calculate my Korean age?
Take the current year, subtract your birth year and add 1. The result is the same whether or not your birthday has passed.

### What does 만 나이 mean?
만 나이 (man nai) is international age: you are 0 at birth and gain a year on each birthday. It is the age you should give on official forms in Korea.

### Why do Koreans ask your age when they first meet you?
Age helps decide which speech level to use and how to address each other, for example whether someone becomes your 언니, 오빠, 형 or 누나.

- [Unified "man nai" age law takes effect (만 나이 통일법 시행): Korea Policy Briefing, korea.kr](https://www.korea.kr/news/policyNewsView.do?newsId=156577051)

Animal vocabulary is some of the first vocabulary Korean children learn: and it is just as fun and useful for adult learners. Beyond the names themselves, Korean has a rich set of onomatopoeia for animal sounds that differ delightfully from English.

## Common Animals in Korean

| Korean | Romanization | English |
|---|---|---|
| 개 | gae | dog |
| 고양이 | goyangi | cat |
| 새 | sae | bird |
| 물고기 | mulgogi | fish |
| 토끼 | tokki | rabbit |
| 곰 | gom | bear |
| 호랑이 | horangi | tiger |
| 사자 | saja | lion |
| 코끼리 | kokkiri | elephant |
| 원숭이 | wonsungi | monkey |
| 여우 | yeou | fox |
| 늑대 | neukdae | wolf |
| 말 | mal | horse |
| 소 | so | cow |
| 돼지 | dwaeji | pig |

## Animal Sounds (의성어): Where Korean Gets Fun

| Animal | Korean sound | English equivalent |
|---|---|---|
| Dog | 멍멍 (meong-meong) | woof woof |
| Cat | 야옹 (yaong) | meow |
| Cow | 음매 (eum-mae) | moo |
| Rooster | 꼬끼오 (kkokkio) | cock-a-doodle-doo |
| Duck | 꽥꽥 (kkwaek-kkwaek) | quack quack |
| Pig | 꿀꿀 (kkul-kkul) | oink oink |
| Frog | 개굴개굴 (gaegul-gaegul) | ribbit ribbit |

Notice how differently Korean hears the same sounds: a rooster says 꼬끼오, not "cock-a-doodle-doo," because languages encode sound differently, not because animals sound different around the world.

## Using Animal Words in Sentences

- 우리 집에는 개가 두 마리 있어요.: I have two dogs at home.
- 고양이가 소파 위에서 자고 있어요.: The cat is sleeping on the sofa.
- 호랑이는 한국의 상징 동물이에요.: The tiger is Korea's symbolic animal.

## Cultural Note: Animals in Korean Idioms

Animals appear constantly in Korean expressions: 원숭이도 나무에서 떨어진다 (even a monkey falls from a tree, meaning even experts make mistakes), and 소 잃고 외양간 고친다 (fixing the barn after losing the cow, meaning closing the barn door after the horse has bolted). Learning animal vocabulary early pays off when you encounter these idioms later.

## Quick FAQ

**Why do animal sounds differ between languages?** Each language's sound system shapes how speakers perceive and represent noises: it's not that animals sound different, but that ears and alphabets interpret sound differently.

**Are animal sounds tested on TOPIK?** Rarely directly, but they appear in children's stories and listening passages used for lower-level TOPIK I content.

Animal vocabulary is some of the first vocabulary Korean children learn: and it is just as fun and useful for adult learners. Beyond the names themselves, Korean has a rich set of onomatopoeia for animal sounds that differ delightfully from English.

## Common Animals in Korean

| Korean | Romanization | English |
|---|---|---|
| 개 | gae | dog |
| 고양이 | goyangi | cat |
| 새 | sae | bird |
| 물고기 | mulgogi | fish |
| 토끼 | tokki | rabbit |
| 곰 | gom | bear |
| 호랑이 | horangi | tiger |
| 사자 | saja | lion |
| 코끼리 | kokkiri | elephant |
| 원숭이 | wonsungi | monkey |
| 여우 | yeou | fox |
| 늑대 | neukdae | wolf |
| 말 | mal | horse |
| 소 | so | cow |
| 돼지 | dwaeji | pig |

## Animal Sounds (의성어): Where Korean Gets Fun

| Animal | Korean sound | English equivalent |
|---|---|---|
| Dog | 멍멍 (meong-meong) | woof woof |
| Cat | 야옹 (yaong) | meow |
| Cow | 음매 (eum-mae) | moo |
| Rooster | 꼬끼오 (kkokkio) | cock-a-doodle-doo |
| Duck | 꽥꽥 (kkwaek-kkwaek) | quack quack |
| Pig | 꿀꿀 (kkul-kkul) | oink oink |
| Frog | 개굴개굴 (gaegul-gaegul) | ribbit ribbit |

Notice how differently Korean hears the same sounds: a rooster says 꼬끼오, not "cock-a-doodle-doo," because languages encode sound differently, not because animals sound different around the world.

## Using Animal Words in Sentences

- 우리 집에는 개가 두 마리 있어요.: I have two dogs at home.
- 고양이가 소파 위에서 자고 있어요.: The cat is sleeping on the sofa.
- 호랑이는 한국의 상징 동물이에요.: The tiger is Korea's symbolic animal.

## Cultural Note: Animals in Korean Idioms

Animals appear constantly in Korean expressions: 원숭이도 나무에서 떨어진다 (even a monkey falls from a tree, meaning even experts make mistakes), and 소 잃고 외양간 고친다 (fixing the barn after losing the cow, meaning closing the barn door after the horse has bolted). Learning animal vocabulary early pays off when you encounter these idioms later.

## Quick FAQ

**Why do animal sounds differ between languages?** Each language's sound system shapes how speakers perceive and represent noises: it's not that animals sound different, but that ears and alphabets interpret sound differently.

**Are animal sounds tested on TOPIK?** Rarely directly, but they appear in children's stories and listening passages used for lower-level TOPIK I content.

## The Gap Between Textbook Korean and Real Korean

Korean textbooks teach you to say 안녕하세요 (hello) and 감사합니다 (thank you). They do not teach you how deep to bow, when to use two hands, or why you should never stick chopsticks upright in rice.

These unwritten rules: 눈치 (nunchi) and social intelligence: are what separate a foreigner who communicates from one who connects.

**Quick answer:** Korean etiquette is built on age and relationship. Greet with a bow, deeper for elders and seniors; give and receive things with two hands; let the oldest person start eating; pour drinks for others, not yourself, and turn slightly away when drinking in front of elders; never stand chopsticks upright in rice; and address colleagues by job title.

## The Bow (인사: Insa)

Bowing is the Korean greeting. But not all bows are equal.

### Bow Depth Guide

| Relationship | Bow Depth | Context |
|-------------|-----------|---------|
| Passing acquaintance | 15° nod | Passing someone in the hallway |
| Meeting someone | 30° | Standard polite greeting |
| Meeting a superior/elder | 45° | Respect or apology |
| Deep apology or extreme respect | 90° | Formal public apology or very senior figures |

### The Two-Hand Rule

When giving or receiving something: a business card, a gift, a drink, money: use TWO hands or support your right arm with your left hand. This shows respect.

One-handed exchanges look careless and rude.

### Do Not Hug
Physical contact between people who are not close is uncommon in Korea. Hugging is reserved for close friends and couples. A handshake is appropriate in business settings with foreigners: but a bow is always safer.

## 눈치 (Nunchi): Reading the Room

눈치 is built on 눈 (eye) and is often glossed as "eye-measure": it is the Korean art of reading situations, emotions, and social dynamics without anyone having to say anything explicitly.

High 눈치: noticing someone is tired and leaving early without being asked.
Low 눈치: missing obvious social cues and making situations awkward.

In Korean culture, being called a 눈치 없는 사람 (nunchi eomneun saram, a person with no nunchi) is a real social criticism. And having good 눈치 is considered a sign of intelligence and emotional maturity.

For foreigners: you are given more grace. But knowing 눈치 exists, and trying to be aware of the room, is appreciated enormously.

## Dining Etiquette

Korean meals have specific rituals that matter deeply.

### Age Eats First
The oldest person at the table sits first, picks up their spoon or chopsticks first, and begins eating first. Younger people wait.

### Pouring Drinks
You do not pour your own drink. You pour for others, and they pour for you. If your glass is full, someone will not pour: finish some first.

When someone older pours for you, receive the glass with two hands.

### The Bill
In Korean culture, treating (사다: sada, "to buy [for someone]") is an expression of affection and care. Arguments over who pays the bill are normal and expected. The most senior person usually pays: but this is not a hard rule among friends.

Splitting bills (더치페이: Dutch pay) is becoming more common among younger Koreans, especially in couples and friend groups.

### Chopstick Rules
- Never stick chopsticks vertically into rice: this resembles the rice offered to the dead at ancestral rites
- Pass food to another person using serving chopsticks or the back of your chopsticks
- Do not wave chopsticks around while talking

### Drinking Culture (술자리: Suljari)
Korean drinking culture is important in social and professional life. Key rules:
- Always pour for others, never yourself
- Turn slightly away and cover your mouth when drinking in front of elders
- Refusing a drink from a senior is difficult: if you do not drink, say so clearly upfront
- 건배 (geonbae) = cheers (literally "dry cup")
- 위하여 (wihayeo) = for the sake of [something/someone]: used in toasts

## Gift Giving

Bringing a gift when visiting someone's home or meeting for the first time is expected.

Good gifts: fruit sets, quality snacks, quality teas, small cosmetics
Avoid: shoes (ending a relationship symbolism), sharp objects like knives (cutting ties)

Gifts are often not opened immediately in front of the giver: this avoids potential awkwardness if the reaction is not enthusiastic enough.

## Age and Hierarchy at Work

Korean workplaces are hierarchical. Your job title matters enormously.

Address colleagues by their title, not their name:
- 부장님 (bujangnim): department manager
- 과장님 (gwajangnim): section chief
- 대리님 (daerinim): assistant manager

Arriving later than your boss is rude. Leaving before your boss leaves is also awkward: many Korean employees wait until their manager goes home.

## Digital Etiquette

Koreans are among the world's most connected people. KakaoTalk is the primary messaging app (like WhatsApp in the Middle East).

- Responding quickly to KakaoTalk messages is expected from colleagues
- Read receipts are visible by default: leaving someone on "read" is noticed
- Voice calls to someone without prior message is considered somewhat rude: text first
- Emojis and stickers are widely used and not seen as unprofessional in many Korean contexts

## One Core Principle

All of Korean social etiquette flows from one principle: **age and relationship determine behavior**.

If you know someone's age and relationship to you, you know how to speak, how deep to bow, who pours for whom, and who pays. This is why Koreans ask your age immediately upon meeting you: they are not being rude. They are gathering the data they need to treat you correctly.

Understanding this makes Korea not just accessible but genuinely fascinating. At Klovers, we teach Korean language and Korean culture together: because one without the other is only half the picture. You can see how it works in a [free trial class](/free-trial).

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How do you bow correctly in Korea?

Bend from the waist with your back straight and your eyes lowered. A light nod of about 15 degrees suits casual encounters, around 30 degrees is a normal polite greeting, and a deeper bow shows extra respect to elders or seniors.

### Why do Koreans use two hands?

Giving or receiving with two hands, or with your left hand supporting your right arm, shows respect. It is expected with elders, seniors and customers, especially for business cards, gifts, money and drinks.

### Is it rude to pour your own drink in Korea?

Traditionally, yes: you pour for others and let them fill your glass. Among close friends it is relaxed, but at work dinners and with elders it still matters.

### Why do Koreans ask your age when they meet you?

Age decides which speech level to use and how people treat each other. Asking is not rude in Korea; it helps the other person speak to you correctly.

Whether you are describing a headache, greeting someone's cute puppy face, or following a K-pop dance tutorial, body part vocabulary comes up constantly. It is also one of the most practical vocabulary sets for real-life situations like visiting a pharmacy in Korea.

## Head and Face

| Korean | Romanization | English |
|---|---|---|
| 머리 | meori | head / hair |
| 얼굴 | eolgul | face |
| 눈 | nun | eye |
| 코 | ko | nose |
| 입 | ip | mouth |
| 귀 | gwi | ear |
| 이/치아 | i/chia | tooth |
| 목 | mok | neck / throat |

## Upper Body

| Korean | Romanization | English |
|---|---|---|
| 어깨 | eokkae | shoulder |
| 팔 | pal | arm |
| 손 | son | hand |
| 손가락 | songarak | finger |
| 가슴 | gaseum | chest |
| 배 | bae | stomach |
| 등 | deung | back |

## Lower Body

| Korean | Romanization | English |
|---|---|---|
| 다리 | dari | leg |
| 무릎 | mureup | knee |
| 발 | bal | foot |
| 발가락 | balgarak | toe |
| 발목 | balmok | ankle |

## Describing Pain: -이/가 아파요

To say a body part hurts, attach the subject particle 이/가 and add 아파요.

- 머리가 아파요.: My head hurts.
- 배가 아파요.: My stomach hurts.
- 목이 아파요.: My throat hurts.
- 다리가 아파요.: My leg hurts.

This single pattern lets you describe almost any ache using the vocabulary above: extremely useful if you ever need a Korean pharmacy (약국) while traveling.

## Quick FAQ

**Is 머리 used for both "head" and "hair"?** Yes: context determines the meaning. "머리를 잘랐어요" means "I cut my hair," not "I cut my head."

**How do I say "I have a cold" in Korean?** 감기에 걸렸어요 (I caught a cold) is the standard phrase, often paired with 목이 아파요 (sore throat) or 콧물이 나요 (runny nose).

Body vocabulary is exactly the kind of everyday, practical language Klovers focuses on: the words you will actually need the moment you land in Korea or chat with a Korean friend.

## Korea's Cafe Obsession

Korea has one of the highest cafe densities in the world. In neighborhoods like Hongdae, Gangnam, and Insadong, it feels like there is a coffee shop on every corner: and not just any coffee shop. Korean cafes are experiences: architectural spaces, themed environments, and culinary art galleries that happen to serve excellent coffee.

For a Korean learner, cafes are also the perfect place to practice. Ordering in Korean at a Seoul cafe is one of the most satisfying small victories you will ever have.

---

## Why Korean Cafes Are Different

### 1. The "Cafe as Destination" Culture
Koreans do not just pop into a cafe for a quick espresso. A cafe visit is often a **social event**: meeting friends, studying, taking photos, or simply spending an afternoon. Minimum orders are common (최소 주문액), and long stays are expected.

### 2. Themed Cafes (테마 카페)
Korea pioneered the concept of the themed cafe:
- **Cat cafes (고양이 카페)**: relax with cats who wander freely
- **Dog cafes (강아지 카페)**: cuddle puppies over your latte
- **Book cafes (북카페)**: floor-to-ceiling bookshelves, reading nooks
- **Forest cafes (숲 카페)**: glass houses surrounded by trees and plants
- **Retro cafes (레트로 카페)**: 1980s–90s aesthetic with vintage games and props

### 3. Seasonal and Visual Menus
Korean cafes compete fiercely on **visual appeal**. Expect:
- Lattes shaped like animals
- Seasonal drinks (cherry blossom latte in spring, sweet potato latte in fall)
- Desserts designed to be photographed before eating
- Signature drinks you cannot find anywhere else

---

## Essential Korean Cafe Vocabulary

### Drinks (음료)

| Korean | Romanization | Meaning |
|--------|-------------|---------|
| 아메리카노 | Americano | Black espresso + water (most popular in Korea) |
| 카페라떼 | Cafe latte | Espresso + steamed milk |
| 카푸치노 | Cappuccino | Cappuccino |
| 바닐라라떼 | Vanilla latte | Vanilla latte |
| 카라멜 마끼아또 | Caramel macchiato | Caramel macchiato |
| 녹차라떼 | Nokcha latte | Green tea latte |
| 달고나라떼 | Dalgona latte | Whipped coffee latte (went viral globally) |
| 플랫화이트 | Flat white | Flat white |
| 에스프레소 | Espresso | Espresso |
| 콜드브루 | Cold brew | Cold brew coffee |

### Temperature Choices

| Korean | Romanization | Meaning |
|--------|-------------|---------|
| 아이스 | Ice | Iced (add before any drink name) |
| 핫 | Hot | Hot (add before any drink name) |
| 따뜻하게요 | Ttatteutage yo | Make it hot, please |
| 차갑게요 | Chagapge yo | Make it cold, please |

> **Tip:** Koreans often just say **아아** (aa): short for 아이스 아메리카노: the most ordered drink in Korea. It is consumed year-round, even in January.

### Ordering Phrases

| Korean | Romanization | Meaning |
|--------|-------------|---------|
| 아이스 아메리카노 한 잔 주세요 | Ice Americano han jan juseyo | One iced Americano, please |
| 여기서 마실게요 | Yeogiseo masil geyo | I'll have it here (for here) |

Causative verbs express that someone made, let, or had someone else do an action: "I fed the baby" (made the baby eat) rather than "I ate." Korean has two main ways to build this, similar in structure to the passive voice.

## The -이/히/리/기/우 Causative Suffixes

A set of common verbs form the causative by adding a suffix directly to the stem: notice these overlap with the passive suffixes, so context determines meaning.

| Base verb | Meaning | Causative form | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| 먹다 | to eat | 먹이다 | to feed (make eat) |
| 입다 | to wear | 입히다 | to dress (make wear) |
| 울다 | to cry | 울리다 | to make cry |
| 씻다 | to wash | 씻기다 | to bathe (make wash) |
| 자다 | to sleep | 재우다 | to put to sleep |

## The -게 하다 Causative: The Productive Pattern

For most other verbs, attach -게 하다 to the verb stem to mean "make/let someone do."

| Base verb | Causative form | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 가다 (to go) | 가게 하다 | to make/let someone go |
| 공부하다 (to study) | 공부하게 하다 | to make someone study |
| 웃다 (to laugh) | 웃게 하다 | to make someone laugh |

## Causative in Context

- 엄마가 아이에게 밥을 먹였어요.: The mom fed the child (made the child eat).
- 선생님이 학생들을 공부하게 했어요.: The teacher made the students study.
- 그 영화가 저를 울렸어요.: That movie made me cry.

## Causative vs Passive: How to Tell Them Apart

Since suffixes like -이, -히, -리, -기 form both passive and causative verbs, context and the sentence's subject/object structure decide the meaning: 먹이다 (feed) is causative because the subject actively causes the action, while 먹히다 (be eaten) is passive because the subject undergoes the action.

## Quick FAQ

**Which pattern should beginners learn first?** -게 하다: it works with nearly any verb and is far easier to apply consistently than memorizing individual causative suffixes.

**Does 시키다 also mean "make someone do"?** Yes: 시키다 (to order/have someone do) is a separate, very common causative-adjacent verb often attached to nouns: 공부시키다 (to make someone study), 청소시키다 (to make someone clean).

Causative and passive verbs often confuse learners because they look similar: Klovers' grammar-focused lessons drill the difference with real examples until it becomes second nature.

## Describing an Outfit

| Korean | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 예뻐요 | pretty |
| 멋있어요 | cool / stylish |
| 편해요 | comfortable |

Example: 이 옷이 정말 잘 어울려요! (This outfit really suits you!): one of the most common compliments in Korean.

## Shopping Phrases You Will Actually Use

- 이거 얼마예요?: How much is this?

## K-Fashion Vocabulary

| Term | Meaning |

| 하객룩 | wedding-guest outfit: a genre of its own in Korean fashion content |

## Quick FAQ

**Is 옷 used for a single item or clothes in general?** 옷 generally means "clothes" as a category: for a specific item, Koreans usually name the item directly (티셔츠, 바지, etc.).

Colors are everywhere in daily conversation, from describing clothes to picking a paint swatch. Korean color vocabulary has a small twist that trips up beginners: many colors function as descriptive verbs (irregular ㅎ adjectives), not simple nouns like in English.

## Basic Colors in Korean

| Korean | Romanization | English |
|---|---|---|
| 빨간색 | ppalgansaek | red |
| 파란색 | paransaek | blue |
| 노란색 | noransaek | yellow |
| 초록색 | choroksaek | green |
| 주황색 | juhwangsaek | orange |
| 보라색 | borasaek | purple |
| 분홍색 | bunhongsaek | pink |
| 검은색 | geomeunsaek | black |
| 흰색 | huinsaek | white |
| 갈색 | galsaek | brown |
| 회색 | hoesaek | gray |
| 금색 | geumsaek | gold |
| 은색 | eunsaek | silver |

Most color nouns end in 색 (saek), meaning "color": 빨간색 literally means "red color." To describe something directly, use the descriptive verb instead (파랗다 → 파래요): 하늘이 파래요 (The sky is blue).

## Color Adjectives Conjugate Like ㅎ Irregulars

Basic color adjectives (빨갛다, 파랗다, 노랗다, 하얗다, 까맣다) follow the ㅎ irregular pattern: the ㅎ disappears and the vowel changes before -어요.

| Dictionary form | Meaning | -어요 form |
|---|---|---|
| 빨갛다 | to be red | 빨개요 |
| 파랗다 | to be blue | 파래요 |
| 노랗다 | to be yellow | 노래요 |
| 하얗다 | to be white | 하얘요 |
| 까맣다 | to be black | 까매요 |

## Cultural Meaning of Colors in Korea

- **Red (빨간색):** Traditionally used to ward off evil spirits; also associated with passion and, in modern contexts, political parties.
- **White (흰색):** Symbolizes purity and is closely tied to Korea's nickname "the land of white-clad people" (백의민족).
- **Gold (금색):** Represents wealth, prosperity, and royalty: commonly seen in hanbok and palace decor.
- **Blue and red together:** Found on the Korean flag (태극기), symbolizing balance between opposing forces (음양, yin-yang).

## Quick FAQ

**Why do some colors end in 색 and others don't?** 색 is the general suffix for naming a color as a noun. Verb forms like 빨갛다 describe something being that color directly, without needing 색.

**Is 파란색 used for both blue and green?** Traditionally yes: older Korean grouped blue and green together, which is why 파란불 (a "blue" traffic light) actually refers to the green light. Modern Korean now distinguishes 초록색 for green more clearly.

| 은색 | eunsaek | silver |

Most color nouns end in 색 (saek), meaning "color": 빨간색 literally means "red color." To describe something directly, use the descriptive verb instead (파랗다 → 파래요): 하늘이 파래요 (The sky is blue).

## Color Adjectives Conjugate Like ㅎ Irregulars

Basic color adjectives (빨갛다, 파랗다, 노랗다, 하얗다, 까맣다) follow the ㅎ irregular pattern: the ㅎ disappears and the vowel changes before -어요.

|---|---|---|

| 파랗다 | to be blue | 파래요 |
| 노랗다 | to be yellow | 노래요 |
| 하얗다 | to be white | 하얘요 |
| 까맣다 | to be black | 까매요 |

## Cultural Meaning of Colors in Korea

- **Red (빨간색):** Traditionally used to ward off evil spirits; also associated with passion and, in modern contexts, political parties.
- **White (흰색):** Symbolizes purity and is closely tied to Korea's nickname "the land of white-clad people" (백의민족).
- **Gold (금색):** Represents wealth, prosperity, and royalty: commonly seen in hanbok and palace decor.
- **Blue and red together:** Found on the Korean flag (태극기), symbolizing balance between opposing forces (음양, yin-yang).

## Quick FAQ

**Why do some colors end in 색 and others don't?** 색 is the general suffix for naming a color as a noun. Verb forms like 빨갛다 describe something being that color directly, without needing 색.

**Is 파란색 used for both blue and green?** Traditionally yes: older Korean grouped blue and green together, which is why 파란불 (a "blue" traffic light) actually refers to the green light. Modern Korean now distinguishes 초록색 for green more clearly.

If you have started building Korean sentences, you have probably wondered why Korean seems to have more than one way to say "if." Korean conditional sentences are essential for everyday conversation, K-drama dialogue, and the TOPIK exam. This guide breaks down the two most common conditional markers, **-으면** and **-다면**, so you can use them naturally and correctly.

## The Everyday Conditional: -으면 (eumyeon)

-으면 attaches to verb and adjective stems to mean "if" or "when." It covers general truths, habits, and realistic conditions: the conditional you will use the most in daily life.

| Stem ends in | Ending | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|
| Consonant | -으면 | 먹으면 (meogeumyeon) | if I eat |
| Vowel | -면 | 가면 (gamyeon) | if I go |
| ㄹ verb | -면 | 살면 (salmyeon) | if I live |

Examples:
- 비가 오면 집에 있어요. (biga omyeon jibe isseoyo): If it rains, I stay home.
- 시간이 있으면 전화해 주세요.: If you have time, please call me.
- 열심히 공부하면 한국어를 잘할 수 있어요.: If you study hard, you can get good at Korean.

## The Hypothetical Conditional: -다면 (damyeon)

-다면 also translates as "if," but it leans toward hypothetical, unlikely, or emotionally loaded situations: closer to "if it were the case that..." You will hear it constantly in K-drama confrontations, because it adds emotional weight to a "what if."

| Situation | Example | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| Hypothetical wish | 복권에 당첨된다면 여행을 갈 거예요. | If I won the lottery, I would travel. |
| Past hypothetical | 그때 알았다면 다르게 행동했을 거예요. | If I had known then, I would have acted differently. |
| Dramatic confrontation | 네가 떠난다면 나는 어떻게 해? | If you leave, what am I supposed to do? |

## -으면 vs -다면 at a Glance

| | -으면 | -다면 |
|---|---|---|
| Tone | Neutral, everyday | Hypothetical, dramatic |
| Best for | Habits, real conditions | Wishes, unlikely "what ifs" |
| TOPIK frequency | Very high | Moderate |

## Common Mistakes to Avoid

1. **Confusing -으면 with -으니까.** -으니까 means "because," not "if": one of the most frequent beginner mix-ups.
2. **Forgetting irregular stems.** Verbs ending in ㄹ (like 살다, to live) behave differently across endings: always double-check the irregular conjugation chart before writing a new sentence type.
3. **Overusing -다면 in casual speech.** Native speakers reserve -다면 for reflective or dramatic contexts. For everyday requests and small talk, -으면 is almost always the safer, more natural choice.

## Quick FAQ

**Is -으면 formal or casual?** Neither: it is neutral and works in both polite (해요체) and formal (합니다체) sentences depending on the ending verb.

**Can I use -다면 with the present tense only?** No. -다면 can attach after present, past (-았/었다면), and future forms, which is exactly what makes it flexible for hypotheticals about the past.

**Which one appears more on TOPIK?** -으면 appears far more often in TOPIK I and II reading and listening sections because it describes realistic, everyday conditions.

## Practice It Yourself

Try translating: "If you are tired, take a rest." "If the weather is nice, let's go outside." Building conditional sentences is one of the fastest ways to sound more natural in Korean, and it unlocks much more advanced grammar down the line.

In Korea, 편의점 (pyeoneuijeom, "convenience store") is far more than a place to grab snacks: it is a genuine cultural institution, open 24 hours, on nearly every corner, and central to daily student and worker life.

## Key Vocabulary

| Korean | Romanization | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 편의점 | pyeoneuijeom | convenience store |
| 삼각김밥 | samgak gimbap | triangle-shaped rice roll snack |
| 도시락 | dosirak | boxed meal |
| 컵라면 | keomnamyeon | cup noodles |
| 파라솔 | parasol | the outdoor tables/umbrellas outside stores |
| 포인트 카드 | pointeu kadeu | loyalty/points card |

## The Big Three Chains

Korea's convenience store landscape is dominated by CU, GS25, and 7-Eleven, each with their own exclusive snacks, meal deals, and seasonal collaborations with popular characters or K-pop groups: collector culture around limited snacks is a real phenomenon.

## Why Convenience Stores Are a Lifestyle Hub

- **Cheap, fast meals:** 도시락 (boxed meals) and 삼각김밥 cost a fraction of a restaurant meal and are a staple for students and office workers on tight schedules.
- **Outdoor seating (파라솔):** Many stores have plastic tables and chairs outside, becoming an informal, affordable spot to eat, drink, and chat with friends late into the night.
- **ATM and bill payment:** Convenience stores double as mini banking hubs, letting people withdraw cash or pay utility bills at any hour.
- **Free hot water for cup noodles:** Nearly every store has a hot water dispenser specifically for preparing instant noodles on the spot.

## Ordering and Shopping Phrases

- 이거 데워주세요.: Please heat this up.
- 봉투 필요해요.: I need a bag.
- 포인트 있으세요?: Do you have a points card?
- 여기서 먹을 수 있어요?: Can I eat here?

## Quick FAQ

**Are convenience stores really open 24/7?** The vast majority are, making them a reliable option for late-night snacks, emergency purchases, or a quick meal after a long night out.

**Is convenience store food actually good?** It has a genuine reputation for quality and variety, with rotating seasonal menus that Koreans actively follow and compare between chains.

Everyday spaces like 편의점 are where real Korean conversation happens. Klovers' practical vocabulary lessons prepare you for exactly these small, constant daily interactions.

## Why Greetings Matter in Korean

Korean culture places deep value on respect and social relationships, and greetings reflect that beautifully. The way you say hello, thank you, or goodbye in Korean changes based on **who you are speaking to**: a stranger, a friend, or a boss. Getting greetings right will immediately impress native speakers and open doors.

---

## Essential Hellos

| Korean | Romanization | Meaning | When to Use |
|--------|-------------|---------|-------------|
| 안녕하세요 | Annyeonghaseyo | Hello (formal) | Strangers, older people, teachers |
| 안녕 | Annyeong | Hi (informal) | Close friends, younger people |
| 안녕하십니까 | Annyeonghasimnikka | Hello (very formal) | Business, military, presentations |
| 반갑습니다 | Bangapseumnida | Nice to meet you | First meetings (formal) |
| 반가워요 | Bangawoyo | Nice to meet you | First meetings (polite) |
| 오랜만이에요 | Oraenmanieyo | Long time no see | Seeing someone after a while |

---

## Goodbyes

Korean has two different "goodbye" expressions depending on who is staying and who is leaving:

| Korean | Romanization | Meaning |
|--------|-------------|---------|
| 안녕히 가세요 | Annyeonghi gaseyo | Goodbye (said to person leaving) |
| 안녕히 계세요 | Annyeonghi gyeseyo | Goodbye (said to person staying) |
| 잘 가요 | Jal gayo | Take care / Bye (casual, to person leaving) |
| 잘 있어요 | Jal isseoyo | Take care (casual, to person staying) |
| 또 봐요 | Tto bwayo | See you again (polite) |
| 나중에 봐요 | Najunge bwayo | See you later |
| 조심히 가세요 | Josimhi gaseyo | Go safely (caring farewell) |

---

## Thank You & Apologies

| Korean | Romanization | Meaning |
|--------|-------------|---------|
| 감사합니다 | Gamsahamnida | Thank you (formal) |
| 고마워요 | Gomawoyo | Thank you (polite) |
| 고마워 | Gomawo | Thanks (casual) |
| 천만에요 | Cheonmaneyo | You're welcome |
| 괜찮아요 | Gwaenchanayo | It's okay / No problem |
| 미안해요 | Mianhaeyo | Sorry (polite) |
| 죄송합니다 | Joesonghamnida | I'm very sorry (formal) |
| 실례합니다 | Sillyehamnida | Excuse me (formal) |

---

## Useful Daily Phrases

| Korean | Romanization | Meaning |
|--------|-------------|---------|
| 네 | Ne | Yes |
| 아니요 | Aniyo | No |
| 맞아요 | Majayo | That's right |
| 모르겠어요 | Moreugesseoyo | I don't know |
| 이해했어요 | Ihaehaesseoyo | I understood |
| 다시 말해 주세요 | Dasi malhae juseyo | Please say that again |
| 천천히 말해 주세요 | Cheoncheonhi malhae juseyo | Please speak slowly |
| 한국어를 조금 해요 | Hangugeoreul jogeum haeyo | I speak a little Korean |
| 영어 하세요? | Yeongeo haseyo? | Do you speak English? |
| 화장실이 어디예요? | Hwajangsiri eodiyeyo? | Where is the bathroom? |

---

## Eating and Food Phrases

| Korean | Romanization | Meaning |
|--------|-------------|---------|
| 잘 먹겠습니다 | Jal meokgesseumnida | I will eat well (before meal) |
| 잘 먹었습니다 | Jal meogeosseumnida | I ate well (after meal) |
| 맛있어요 | Masisseoyo | It's delicious |
| 얼마예요? | Eolmayeyo? | How much is it? |
| 주세요 | Juseyo | Please give me... |
| 하나 더 주세요 | Hana deo juseyo | One more, please |

---

## Phone and Text

| Korean | Romanization | Meaning |
|--------|-------------|---------|
| 여보세요 | Yeoboseyo | Hello (on the phone only) |
| 잠깐만요 | Jamkkanmanyo | Just a moment |
| 나중에 전화할게요 | Najunge jeonhwahalgeyo | I'll call you later |

---

## Pro Tips for Using Korean Greetings

1. **Bow when greeting**: a slight nod or bow shows respect, especially with formal speech levels.
2. **Use formal speech by default** when unsure: Koreans appreciate the effort.
3. **잘 먹겠습니다** before every meal, even at a restaurant: it shows appreciation.
4. **여보세요 is only for phone calls**: never use it as a face-to-face greeting.
5. **안녕하세요 is your Swiss army knife**: it works in almost any situation with anyone you don't know.

Practice these phrases daily and you'll feel the difference in how Koreans respond to you. Start your structured Korean journey today!

Getting lost is part of traveling, but knowing how to ask for and understand directions in Korean turns a stressful moment into a manageable one. This vocabulary is some of the most immediately useful Korean you can learn.

## Basic Direction Words

| Korean | Romanization | English |
|---|---|---|
| 왼쪽 | oenjjok | left |
| 오른쪽 | oreunjjok | right |
| 앞 | ap | front |
| 뒤 | dwi | back |
| 위 | wi | above/on top |
| 아래/밑 | arae/mit | below/under |
| 옆 | yeop | next to/beside |
| 근처 | geuncheo | nearby |

## Movement Verbs for Directions

| Korean | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 직진하다 | to go straight |
| 돌다 | to turn |
| 건너다 | to cross |
| 나오다 | to come out (of a station/building) |

## Asking for Directions

- 여기가 어디예요?: Where am I?
- 화장실이 어디예요?: Where is the bathroom?
- 이 근처에 편의점 있어요?: Is there a convenience store nearby?
- 지하철역까지 어떻게 가요?: How do I get to the subway station?

## Giving and Understanding Directions

- 직진하세요.: Go straight.
- 왼쪽으로 도세요.: Turn left.
- 오른쪽으로 도세요.: Turn right.
- 두 번째 골목에서 왼쪽으로 가세요.: Turn left at the second alley.
- 편의점 옆에 있어요.: It's next to the convenience store.

## Useful Landmark Vocabulary

| Korean | Meaning |
|---|---|
| 사거리 | intersection |
| 신호등 | traffic light |
| 골목 | alley |
| 건물 | building |
| 출구 | exit (as in subway exits, numbered) |

Subway exits in Korea are numbered (1번 출구, 2번 출구), so directions are often given relative to a specific exit number rather than compass directions.

## Quick FAQ

**Is it common for locals to walk you to a location instead of explaining?** Yes: many Koreans will walk with you part of the way rather than give complicated verbal directions, especially if the route is confusing.

**Are map apps reliable in Korea?** Google Maps has limited functionality for walking/driving directions in Korea; locals mostly rely on Naver Map or Kakao Map instead.

Knowing this vocabulary means you can actually navigate a new city with confidence. Klovers' practical lessons prepare you for exactly these real-world situations.

## Beyond Basic K-Drama Vocabulary

You already know daebak and jinjja. Now level up with intermediate and advanced vocabulary.

**Quick answer:** Advanced K-drama vocabulary goes beyond 대박 (daebak) and 진짜 (jinjja) into words tied to each genre: 설레다 (to flutter) and 짝사랑 (one-sided love) in romance, 사직서 (resignation letter) and 승진 (promotion) in office dramas, 용의자 (suspect) and 수사 (investigation) in thrillers, and 유산 (inheritance) and 재벌 (chaebol) in family dramas.

## Romance Drama Vocabulary

Key words for love stories: seolleda (flutter), jjaksarang (one-sided love), mildang (push and pull), gobaek (confession).

## Workplace Drama Vocabulary

Business terms: sajikseo (resignation letter), seungjin (promotion), haego (dismissal, being fired), baesin (betrayal).

## Crime/Thriller Vocabulary

Mystery terms: yonguija (suspect), beomin (criminal), sageon (case), susa (investigation).

## Family Drama Vocabulary

Family terms: yusan (inheritance), jaebeol (chaebol), hyodo (filial piety).

## Dramatic Expressions

Phrases that appear in nearly every drama.

## Example Sentences From Each Genre

Here is how the words above and some classic dramatic lines sound in real sentences. Say each one aloud and listen for it in the next drama you watch.

| Korean | Romanization | Meaning | Genre |
|--------|--------------|---------|-------|
| 가슴이 설레요. | gaseumi seolleyo | My heart is fluttering. | Romance |
| 고백할 거야. | gobaekal geoya | I'm going to confess my feelings. | Romance |
| 짝사랑이었어. | jjaksarang-ieosseo | It was a one-sided love. | Romance |
| 사직서를 냈어요. | sajikseoreul naesseoyo | I handed in my resignation letter. | Workplace |
| 승진했어요! | seungjinhaesseoyo | I got promoted! | Workplace |
| 당신은 해고야. | dangsineun haegoya | You're fired. | Workplace |
| 용의자가 누구예요? | yonguijaga nuguyeyo | Who is the suspect? | Crime |
| 범인은 이 안에 있어. | beomineun i ane isseo | The culprit is in this room. | Crime |
| 유산은 다 내 거야. | yusaneun da nae geoya | The inheritance is all mine. | Family |
| 어떻게 나한테 이럴 수 있어? | eotteoke nahante ireol su isseo | How could you do this to me? | Dramatic |
| 거짓말하지 마. | geojinmalhaji ma | Don't lie to me. | Dramatic |
| 가지 마. | gaji ma | Don't go. | Dramatic |
| 미안해. 다 내 잘못이야. | mianhae. da nae jalmosiya | I'm sorry. It's all my fault. | Dramatic |
| 배신이야. | baesiniya | This is betrayal. | Dramatic |

Notice that most of these lines use casual speech (반말), because drama characters shout them at people they are close to. In real life, use the polite -요 form with people you don't know well.

## Beyond Basic K-Drama Vocabulary

You already know daebak and jinjja. Now level up with intermediate and advanced vocabulary.

**Quick answer:** Advanced K-drama vocabulary goes beyond 대박 (daebak) and 진짜 (jinjja) into words tied to each genre: 설레다 (to flutter) and 짝사랑 (one-sided love) in romance, 사직서 (resignation letter) and 승진 (promotion) in office dramas, 용의자 (suspect) and 수사 (investigation) in thrillers, and 유산 (inheritance) and 재벌 (chaebol) in family dramas.

## Romance Drama Vocabulary

Key words for love stories: seolleda (flutter), jjaksarang (one-sided love), mildang (push and pull), gobaek (confession).

## Workplace Drama Vocabulary

Business terms: sajikseo (resignation letter), seungjin (promotion), haego (dismissal, being fired), baesin (betrayal).

## Crime/Thriller Vocabulary

Mystery terms: yonguija (suspect), beomin (criminal), sageon (case), susa (investigation).

## Family Drama Vocabulary

Family terms: yusan (inheritance), jaebeol (chaebol), hyodo (filial piety).

## Dramatic Expressions

Phrases that appear in nearly every drama.

## Example Sentences From Each Genre

Here is how the words above and some classic dramatic lines sound in real sentences. Say each one aloud and listen for it in the next drama you watch.

|--------|--------------|---------|-------|
| 가슴이 설레요. | gaseumi seolleyo | My heart is fluttering. | Romance |
| 고백할 거야. | gobaekal geoya | I'm going to confess my feelings. | Romance |
| 짝사랑이었어. | jjaksarang-ieosseo | It was a one-sided love. | Romance |
| 사직서를 냈어요. | sajikseoreul naesseoyo | I handed in my resignation letter. | Workplace |
| 승진했어요! | seungjinhaesseoyo | I got promoted! | Workplace |
| 당신은 해고야. | dangsineun haegoya | You're fired. | Workplace |
| 용의자가 누구예요? | yonguijaga nuguyeyo | Who is the suspect? | Crime |
| 범인은 이 안에 있어. | beomineun i ane isseo | The culprit is in this room. | Crime |
| 유산은 다 내 거야. | yusaneun da nae geoya | The inheritance is all mine. | Family |
| 어떻게 나한테 이럴 수 있어? | eotteoke nahante ireol su isseo | How could you do this to me? | Dramatic |
| 거짓말하지 마. | geojinmalhaji ma | Don't lie to me. | Dramatic |
| 가지 마. | gaji ma | Don't go. | Dramatic |
| 미안해. 다 내 잘못이야. | mianhae. da nae jalmosiya | I'm sorry. It's all my fault. | Dramatic |

Notice that most of these lines use casual speech (반말), because drama characters shout them at people they are close to. In real life, use the polite -요 form with people you don't know well.

## Quick Reference: kdrama vocabulary

Keep this mini-cheatsheet for kdrama vocabulary. Practice the key phrases aloud for five minutes every morning, and re-read this guide once a week. Consistency beats intensity: short daily reps build lasting fluency faster than weekend marathons.

## Frequently Asked Questions

### How long before I see real progress with kdrama vocabulary?
Progress depends on how often you practise. If you review a little every day and meet the same words again in real Korean, you will recognise and use them much sooner than with occasional long study sessions.

### What resources pair best with this guide?
Combine this article with a live class, a short daily writing habit, and one K-drama scene a day. Together they cover speaking, writing and listening.

### Should I focus on speaking or grammar first?
Grammar gives you the scaffolding, but speaking forces the brain to retrieve language under pressure. Beginners should do both: 30 minutes of grammar, 15 minutes of shadowing speech: every single day.

## For Arabic-Speaking Learners

Arabic speakers already have useful habits for tackling kdrama vocabulary: you are used to learning a new script, and Arabic also attaches small grammatical pieces to words, much as Korean attaches particles such as 은/는 and 이/가. Korean sounds and word order are still very different, so learn each item with its Hangul spelling and an example sentence. Our [courses](/courses) are available in Arabic, so explanations and comparisons come in your own language.

## Next Steps

If this guide helped, take two minutes right now. First, bookmark this page so you can revisit it. Second, try our free [placement test](/placement-test) to see exactly where you stand. Third, join our community of Arabic-speaking Korean learners: studying alone works, but studying with accountability works faster. Every fluent Korean speaker started where you are right now.

Sharing drinks is a core part of Korean social life, from casual nights with friends to mandatory work dinners. Soju, Korea's signature spirit, comes with its own set of unwritten etiquette rules: breaking them, even by accident, can seem disrespectful to older or more senior drinking partners.

## Key Vocabulary

| Korean | Romanization | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 소주 | soju | Korea's signature clear spirit |
| 건배 | geonbae | cheers / toast |
| 회식 | hoesik | company dinner/drinking event |
| 원샷 | wonsyat | "one shot," drink it all at once |
| 술자리 | suljari | a drinking gathering |
| 폭탄주 | poktanju | "bomb shot": soju mixed with beer |

## The Golden Rules of Pouring

1. **Never pour your own drink.** Someone else should always pour for you, and you pour for others: it is considered a small act of care and respect.
2. **Use two hands when pouring for elders.** Support the bottle with one hand and hold your wrist or forearm with the other as a sign of respect.
3. **Hold your glass with two hands when receiving from an elder.** One hand on the glass, the other lightly supporting your forearm.
4. **Refill glasses before they are empty.** Watching a companion's glass and refilling it proactively is considered good etiquette.

## Turning Away to Drink

When drinking with someone significantly older or more senior, it is traditional to turn your head slightly away from them as you drink: a subtle gesture of respect that surprises many first-time visitors.

## 회식 (Hoesik): The Company Dinner

Hoesik are work dinners, often involving several rounds at different venues, that build team bonds outside the office. While drinking culture around hoesik has relaxed significantly in recent years, understanding the tradition explains a lot of Korean workplace dynamics you will see referenced in dramas and shows.

## Quick FAQ

**Is it rude to refuse a drink?** Not anymore: modern etiquette accepts a polite refusal, though older-generation settings may still expect at least a symbolic first drink.

**What is 원샷?** A call to drink your entire glass in one go, common during toasts, celebrations, or games at a 술자리.

**Do these rules apply to beer and wine too?** The two-hand pouring and receiving etiquette generally applies to any alcohol shared with someone senior, not just soju specifically.

Understanding social customs like these helps you navigate real Korean social situations with confidence.

Korea's education system is famous for producing some of the highest test scores in the world: and infamous for the intense pressure it puts on students. At the center of this system is 학원 (hagwon), the private after-school academies that shape daily life for millions of Korean students.

## What Is a Hagwon (학원)?

A hagwon is a private, for-profit academy that students attend after regular school hours, covering everything from math and English to art and music. Unlike optional tutoring in many countries, hagwon attendance is very common among Korean students, especially in cities like Seoul.

## Key Vocabulary

| Korean | Romanization | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 학원 | hagwon | private academy |
| 학교 | hakgyo | school |
| 수능 | suneung | the national college entrance exam |
| 야자 (야간자율학습) | yaja | supervised evening self-study at school |
| 입시 | ipsi | the college entrance process |
| 학원비 | hagwonbi | academy tuition fees |

## A Typical Student's Day

Many Korean high school students attend regular school from around 8 AM to 4 PM, then move directly to one or more hagwon sessions until 9 or 10 PM, followed by homework late into the night. This routine repeats through most of the school year, intensifying dramatically in the final year before 수능.

## 수능 (Suneung): The Exam That Shapes a Nation

Suneung, held on a single day each November, is so significant that flights are rerouted during the listening test, offices open later to ease traffic for test-takers, and younger students often bow outside test centers to wish exam-takers luck. A single day's score heavily influences university admission, and by extension, many students' career trajectories.

## Why This Culture Exists

Education is deeply tied to social mobility and family honor in Korea, and competition for spots at top universities (often called SKY: Seoul National, Korea, and Yonsei University) is intense. Hagwon culture grew directly out of this pressure, as families invest heavily to give their children any possible advantage.

## Quick FAQ

**Do all Korean students attend hagwon?** Not universally, but attendance is extremely common, particularly in academically competitive regions, and rates increase sharply as students approach high school.

**Is hagwon culture changing?** Yes: government reforms have tried to cap late-night hagwon hours and reduce pressure, though the underlying competition for university spots remains intense.

**Is this reflected in K-dramas?** Frequently: many popular dramas explore hagwon culture and suneung pressure as central plot themes, reflecting real anxieties many Korean families share.

Understanding hagwon culture gives real context to countless K-drama storylines and everyday conversations about Korean family life. Klovers brings this kind of cultural depth into every course, not just grammar drills.

## Why Korean Family Terms Are Uniquely Complex

In English, "uncle" covers your mother's brother, your father's brother, and your parents' friends you were told to call uncle. In Korean, each of these has a different, specific word.

**Quick answer:** Korean family terms change with the side of the family and often with the speaker's gender. A woman calls her older brother 오빠 and older sister 언니; a man says 형 and 누나. Your father's sister is 고모, your mother's sister is 이모, your mother's brother is 외삼촌, and maternal grandparents take the prefix 외-.

Korean family terminology is one of the most intricate in the world: and one of the most revealing about Korean culture. The number of distinct terms reflects how seriously Korea takes family relationships and hierarchical positioning.

More interestingly: **many Korean family terms depend on the speaker's gender**, not just the relationship. A woman calls her older brother 오빠 (oppa). A man calls his older brother 형 (hyeong). Same relationship, different word.

## The Core Family Terms

### Parents and Grandparents

| Relationship | Korean | Romanization | Notes |
|-------------|--------|-------------|-------|
| Father | 아버지 | abeoji | formal |
| Father | 아빠 | appa | casual (like "dad") |
| Mother | 어머니 | eomeoni | formal |
| Mother | 엄마 | eomma | casual (like "mom") |
| Grandfather (pat.) | 할아버지 | harabeoji | father's father |
| Grandmother (pat.) | 할머니 | halmeoni | father's mother |
| Grandfather (mat.) | 외할아버지 | oeharabeoji | mother's father |
| Grandmother (mat.) | 외할머니 | oehalmeoni | mother's mother |

### Siblings: The Gender-Dependent Terms

This is where it gets interesting.

**If you are female:**
| Relationship | Korean | Romanization |
|-------------|--------|-------------|
| Older brother | 오빠 | oppa |
| Older sister | 언니 | eonni |
| Younger sibling (any) | 동생 | dongsaeng |

**If you are male:**
| Relationship | Korean | Romanization |
|-------------|--------|-------------|
| Older brother | 형 | hyeong |
| Older sister | 누나 | nuna |
| Younger sibling (any) | 동생 | dongsaeng |

This is why 오빠 (oppa) has become globally famous through K-Pop: female fans calling male idols "oppa" implies a sibling-like closeness with an older male figure, which carries emotional warmth in Korean culture.

### Extended Family: Paternal vs Maternal

Korean distinguishes between relatives on the father's side and mother's side.

**Father's side:**
| Relationship | Korean | Romanization |
|-------------|--------|-------------|
| Father's older brother | 큰아버지 | keun-abeoji |
| Father's younger brother | 작은아버지 / 삼촌 | jageun-abeoji / samchon |
| Father's sister | 고모 | gomo |
| Father's brother's wife | 큰어머니 / 작은어머니 | keun-eomeoni / jageun-eomeoni |

**Mother's side:**
| Relationship | Korean | Romanization |
|-------------|--------|-------------|
| Mother's brother | 외삼촌 | oesamchon |
| Mother's sister | 이모 | imo |
| Mother's sister's husband | 이모부 | imobu |

### Spouse and In-Laws

| Relationship | Korean | Romanization |
|-------------|--------|-------------|
| Husband | 남편 | nampyeon |
| Wife | 아내 (your own wife) / 부인 (someone else's wife, polite) | anae / buin |
| Father-in-law (husband's father) | 시아버지 | si-abeoji |
| Mother-in-law (husband's mother) | 시어머니 | si-eomeoni |
| Father-in-law (wife's father) | 장인 | jangin |
| Mother-in-law (wife's mother) | 장모 | jangmo |

### More Relatives You Will Hear

| Relationship | Korean | Romanization |
|-------------|--------|-------------|
| Son / daughter | 아들 / 딸 | adeul / ttal |
| Younger brother / younger sister | 남동생 / 여동생 | namdongsaeng / yeodongsaeng |
| Grandson / granddaughter | 손자 / 손녀 | sonja / sonnyeo |
| Cousin | 사촌 | sachon |
| Nephew or niece | 조카 | joka |
| Father's sister's husband | 고모부 | gomobu |
| Mother's brother's wife | 외숙모 | oesungmo |
| Older sister's husband (female speaker) | 형부 | hyeongbu |
| Older sister's husband (male speaker) | 매형 | maehyeong |
| Older brother's wife (female speaker) | 새언니 | saeeonni |
| Older brother's wife (male speaker) | 형수 | hyeongsu |

Two example sentences:
- 저는 오빠 한 명하고 여동생 한 명이 있어요.: I have one older brother and one younger sister (said by a woman).
- 우리 이모는 부산에 살아요.: My aunt (my mother's sister) lives in Busan.

## Why These Terms Matter Beyond Family Conversations

Korean family terms are not just used within families. They are widely used in everyday social life:

**오빠 (oppa)**: Women use this not just for older brothers but for older male friends, boyfriends, and as an affectionate term for any older man they are close to.

**언니 (eonni)**: Women use this for older female friends, mentors, or any older woman they feel close to.

**형 (hyeong)**: Men use this for older male friends, seniors, and mentor figures.

**누나 (nuna)**: Men use this for older female friends or women they admire.

**아저씨 (ajeossi)**: A middle-aged man. Technically accurate but can feel rude: Koreans joke that being called 아저씨 for the first time is a milestone of getting older.

**아줌마 (ajumma)**: A middle-aged woman. Similarly, this feels more like "ma'am" than a compliment.

## 우리 (Uri): "Our" Instead of "My"

One of the most distinctly Korean language features is using 우리 (uri = "our") where English uses "my":

- 우리 엄마: "our mom" (not "my mom")
- 우리 집: "our house" (not "my house")
- 우리나라: "our country" (extremely common)

This reflects the collectivist nature of Korean culture: possession is communal, not individual.

## Practical Usage Tips

1. **Use 어머님/아버님** when talking to someone else about their parents: more respectful than 엄마/아빠.

2. **Never call an older Korean person by their first name**: use a title such as 선생님, their job title, or a kinship term like 언니 or 형 once you are close.

3. **When in doubt about someone's age**: use polite speech and wait for them to signal comfort with informality.

4. **Learning these terms impresses Koreans enormously**: it signals that you understand Korean culture, not just Korean words.

At Klovers, we teach family vocabulary alongside the culture that gives it meaning. Understanding 오빠 and 형 is not just vocabulary: it is understanding how Korean people see relationships and identity. You can practise these terms with a teacher in a [free trial class](/free-trial).

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the difference between oppa and hyeong?
Both mean "older brother". 오빠 (oppa) is used by women and 형 (hyeong) by men, for real brothers and for close older male friends.

### What does imo mean in Korean?
이모 (imo) is your mother's sister. It is also used warmly for older women you are close to, such as a family friend or the owner of a favorite local restaurant.

### How do you say cousin in Korean?
Cousin is 사촌 (sachon). Cousins on the mother's side are often called 외사촌 (oesachon).

### Why do Koreans say 우리 엄마 instead of "my mom"?
Korean usually uses 우리 ("our") for family, home and country, so 우리 엄마 is the natural way to say "my mom" even when you are an only child.

- [호칭어 (Korean terms of address): Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, Academy of Korean Studies](https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0063874)

| Father | 아버지 | abeoji | formal |
| Father | 아빠 | appa | casual (like "dad") |
| Mother | 어머니 | eomeoni | formal |
| Mother | 엄마 | eomma | casual (like "mom") |
| Grandfather (pat.) | 할아버지 | harabeoji | father's father |
| Grandmother (pat.) | 할머니 | halmeoni | father's mother |
| Grandfather (mat.) | 외할아버지 | oeharabeoji | mother's father |
| Grandmother (mat.) | 외할머니 | oehalmeoni | mother's mother |

### Siblings: The Gender-Dependent Terms

This is where it gets interesting.

**If you are female:**
| Relationship | Korean | Romanization |
|-------------|--------|-------------|
| Older brother | 오빠 | oppa |
| Older sister | 언니 | eonni |
| Younger sibling (any) | 동생 | dongsaeng |

**If you are male:**
| Relationship | Korean | Romanization |
|-------------|--------|-------------|
| Older brother | 형 | hyeong |
| Older sister | 누나 | nuna |
| Younger sibling (any) | 동생 | dongsaeng |

This is why 오빠 (oppa) has become globally famous through K-Pop: female fans calling male idols "oppa" implies a sibling-like closeness with an older male figure, which carries emotional warmth in Korean culture.

### Extended Family: Paternal vs Maternal

Korean distinguishes between relatives on the father's side and mother's side.

**Father's side:**
| Relationship | Korean | Romanization |
|-------------|--------|-------------|
| Father's older brother | 큰아버지 | keun-abeoji |
| Father's younger brother | 작은아버지 / 삼촌 | jageun-abeoji / samchon |
| Father's sister | 고모 | gomo |
| Father's brother's wife | 큰어머니 / 작은어머니 | keun-eomeoni / jageun-eomeoni |

**Mother's side:**
| Relationship | Korean | Romanization |
|-------------|--------|-------------|
| Mother's brother | 외삼촌 | oesamchon |
| Mother's sister | 이모 | imo |
| Mother's sister's husband | 이모부 | imobu |

### Spouse and In-Laws

| Relationship | Korean | Romanization |
|-------------|--------|-------------|
| Husband | 남편 | nampyeon |
| Wife | 아내 (your own wife) / 부인 (someone else's wife, polite) | anae / buin |
| Father-in-law (husband's father) | 시아버지 | si-abeoji |
| Mother-in-law (husband's mother) | 시어머니 | si-eomeoni |
| Father-in-law (wife's father) | 장인 | jangin |
| Mother-in-law (wife's mother) | 장모 | jangmo |

### More Relatives You Will Hear

| Relationship | Korean | Romanization |
|-------------|--------|-------------|
| Son / daughter | 아들 / 딸 | adeul / ttal |
| Younger brother / younger sister | 남동생 / 여동생 | namdongsaeng / yeodongsaeng |
| Grandson / granddaughter | 손자 / 손녀 | sonja / sonnyeo |
| Cousin | 사촌 | sachon |
| Nephew or niece | 조카 | joka |
| Father's sister's husband | 고모부 | gomobu |
| Mother's brother's wife | 외숙모 | oesungmo |
| Older sister's husband (female speaker) | 형부 | hyeongbu |
| Older sister's husband (male speaker) | 매형 | maehyeong |
| Older brother's wife (female speaker) | 새언니 | saeeonni |
| Older brother's wife (male speaker) | 형수 | hyeongsu |

Two example sentences:
- 저는 오빠 한 명하고 여동생 한 명이 있어요.: I have one older brother and one younger sister (said by a woman).
- 우리 이모는 부산에 살아요.: My aunt (my mother's sister) lives in Busan.

## Why These Terms Matter Beyond Family Conversations

Korean family terms are not just used within families. They are widely used in everyday social life:

**오빠 (oppa)**: Women use this not just for older brothers but for older male friends, boyfriends, and as an affectionate term for any older man they are close to.

**언니 (eonni)**: Women use this for older female friends, mentors, or any older woman they feel close to.

**형 (hyeong)**: Men use this for older male friends, seniors, and mentor figures.

**누나 (nuna)**: Men use this for older female friends or women they admire.

**아저씨 (ajeossi)**: A middle-aged man. Technically accurate but can feel rude: Koreans joke that being called 아저씨 for the first time is a milestone of getting older.

**아줌마 (ajumma)**: A middle-aged woman. Similarly, this feels more like "ma'am" than a compliment.

## 우리 (Uri): "Our" Instead of "My"

One of the most distinctly Korean language features is using 우리 (uri = "our") where English uses "my":

- 우리 엄마: "our mom" (not "my mom")
- 우리 집: "our house" (not "my house")
- 우리나라: "our country" (extremely common)

This reflects the collectivist nature of Korean culture: possession is communal, not individual.

## Practical Usage Tips

1. **Use 어머님/아버님** when talking to someone else about their parents: more respectful than 엄마/아빠.

2. **Never call an older Korean person by their first name**: use a title such as 선생님, their job title, or a kinship term like 언니 or 형 once you are close.

3. **When in doubt about someone's age**: use polite speech and wait for them to signal comfort with informality.

4. **Learning these terms impresses Koreans enormously**: it signals that you understand Korean culture, not just Korean words.

At Klovers, we teach family vocabulary alongside the culture that gives it meaning. Understanding 오빠 and 형 is not just vocabulary: it is understanding how Korean people see relationships and identity. You can practise these terms with a teacher in a [free trial class](/free-trial).

## Frequently Asked Questions

### What is the difference between oppa and hyeong?
Both mean "older brother". 오빠 (oppa) is used by women and 형 (hyeong) by men, for real brothers and for close older male friends.

### What does imo mean in Korean?
이모 (imo) is your mother's sister. It is also used warmly for older women you are close to, such as a family friend or the owner of a favorite local restaurant.

### How do you say cousin in Korean?
Cousin is 사촌 (sachon). Cousins on the mother's side are often called 외사촌 (oesachon).

### Why do Koreans say 우리 엄마 instead of "my mom"?
Korean usually uses 우리 ("our") for family, home and country, so 우리 엄마 is the natural way to say "my mom" even when you are an only child.

## Sources and further reading

- [호칭어 (Korean terms of address): Encyclopedia of Korean Culture, Academy of Korean Studies](https://encykorea.aks.ac.kr/Article/E0063874)

A baby's first birthday, 돌 (dol), is one of the most celebrated milestones in Korean family life: historically marking survival past a period of high infant mortality, and today a joyful, elaborate family celebration.

## Key Vocabulary

| Korean | Romanization | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| 돌 | dol | first birthday |
| 돌잔치 | doljanchi | first birthday party/celebration |
| 돌잡이 | doljabi | fortune-telling item-picking tradition |
| 한복 | hanbok | traditional clothing (worn by the baby) |
| 백일 | baegil | 100-day celebration (an earlier milestone) |

## Why the First Birthday Matters So Much

In pre-modern Korea, infant mortality rates were high, so surviving to one year old was a genuine milestone worth major celebration: a tradition that continued even as child health dramatically improved, now centered more on joy and family gathering than survival anxiety.

## 돌잡이 (Doljabi): Predicting the Baby's Future

The celebration's most iconic moment is doljabi, where the baby is placed in front of a table of symbolic objects and encouraged to pick one: whichever item they grab is playfully interpreted as a sign of their future path.

| Object | Predicted future |
|---|---|
| 실 (thread) | Long life |
| 돈 (money) | Wealth |
| 쌀 (rice) | Abundance, never going hungry |
| 연필/책 (pencil/book) | Scholarly success |
| 청진기 (stethoscope) | Becoming a doctor |
| 마이크 (microphone) | Becoming a celebrity/entertainer |

Modern doljabi tables often include contemporary items like a golf ball, gavel, or mouse to represent careers in sports, law, or technology.

## Modern Doljanchi Celebrations

Today's doljanchi often resembles a small wedding: a rented event hall, professional photography, a hanbok-clad baby, and a full guest list of family and friends, complete with a celebratory feast and small gift favors for guests.

## Quick FAQ

**Is doljanchi still widely practiced today?** Yes: while the scale varies by family budget and preference, celebrating a baby's first birthday remains a near-universal tradition in Korean families.

**Does the doljabi item actually predict anything?** It's treated affectionately as fun tradition rather than serious fortune telling today, though older generations sometimes take it more seriously.

Family milestones like doljanchi reveal so much warmth and value around children in Korean culture. Klovers' cultural lessons bring context like this into your language learning journey.
